<reflection>
After three experiments, M3 remains the best-fitting model, but M12, M9, M2, M1, M10, and M15 are very close (NLL differences < 0.5). The previous experiment with added product (run_3) did not strongly discriminate among them. My aim for this turn is to design an experiment that specifically tests product-dependent deactivation (M12) versus catalyst deactivation independent of product (M9) and versus no deactivation (M3, M1, M2). By using high catalyst with added product, we can amplify any deactivation effects and observe the time-course shape for early plateaus.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
2. Hypothesis discrimination: The key difference is whether deactivation is accelerated by product (M12) or not (M9), and whether deactivation occurs at all (M3, M1, M2). M12 involves irreversible deactivation by product (P + cat → inactive), so added product directly increases the deactivation rate. M9 involves first-order catalyst deactivation independent of product. M3, M1, and M2 have no deactivation; added product only affects reversibility.

3. Discriminative experiment design: Propose an experiment with high catalyst concentration (0.15 M) and added product (0.2 M), keeping substrate at 2.0 M to match the first experiment (run_1) and isolate the effect of product. This contrasts with run_1 (no product) and run_3 (lower catalyst with product). The high catalyst concentration makes deactivation more pronounced if it depends on catalyst concentration.

4. Contrastive predictions:
   - M12: Deactivation rate is proportional to [P][cat]. With high cat and added P, deactivation is rapid, causing an early plateau at low conversion. The product vs. time curve may show an initial slope that quickly flattens.
   - M9: Deactivation is first-order in cat, independent of P. The curve will resemble run_1 but slowed by reversibility due to added product. It may show a gradual approach to a plateau determined by deactivation and equilibrium, but not as abrupt as M12.
   - M3 (dimer catalysis): No deactivation. Added product slows the initial rate and reduces final conversion due to equilibrium, but the curve will be smooth and asymptotic without an early plateau.
   - M1 and M2: Similar to M3 in terms of no deactivation, but with different rate laws. They predict a smooth reversible approach.
   These differences will be evident in the early curvature and final conversion reached.
</hypothesis>
